target_customer: Music listeners and sharers across streaming services, plus publishers, messaging clients and artists who embed service-agnostic song links and players (Rap Genius was a named partner)
problem: Music links and playlists only work inside one streaming service, so friends on different services cannot easily share or play the same song.
business_model: Free consumer product with a planned small finder's fee on downloads sold through affiliate links, and a hope of monetizing data later
product_category: Cross-service music aggregation, playlists and embeddable player

founders.name: Shehzad Daredia
founders.background_notes: TechCrunch says the founders worked on search problems at Kayak and BillShrink (BillShrink was sold to MasterCard). The source does not say which founder held which job, so both are listed for Daredia and Gomez.

exit.reason: Founders said unifying digital music would need hundreds of millions of dollars in an industry with monetization concerns; service shut down 2015-10-31 after the deal, which looks like an acquihire.

competitors.name: Spotify, Rdio, SoundCloud, YouTube
competitors.what: The single-service players whose catalogs bop.fm aggregated; Rdio and Spotify were hard to embed on websites
competitors.traction_then: Large, but not stated in the source

technical_complexity.rationale: Integrating many service APIs, matching songs across catalogs and building web, iOS and embed players is standard engineering with some hard parts for two founders.

defensibility.rationale: The value depended on third-party APIs and catalogs, there were no exclusive rights, and a streaming service could ship cross-service links itself.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: No incumbent copied it in the sources found; the team was acquired by LifeLock in October 2015 and the product was shut down.

market_need_then: In 2013 listeners were split across Spotify, Rdio, YouTube, SoundCloud and others, and sharing a song across services was awkward. Coverage at the December 2013 launch framed this as the gap bop.fm filled. No usage or revenue numbers were published.

branding.domain_note: Used a .fm domain (bop.fm); no purchase story found.
branding.community_and_virality: Coverage came mainly from music and tech trade press (Hypebot, TNW, Billboard chart integration); no evidence of merch or a fan community.

brand_strength.rationale: Coverage of the product existed but no source shows brand-level recognition, mascot or community; the name was neutral and short.

outcome_analysis: Bop.fm launched out of beta in December 2013 as a cross-service music player and link layer and raised about $2 million in 2014. The founders concluded that building a consumer destination would require hundreds of millions of dollars in an industry with weak monetization, and sold the team to LifeLock in October 2015, shutting the product on October 31. The wedge depended on third-party services and offered little defensibility, so the outcome reads as a soft landing rather than a product success.
notes: bop.fm returned HTTP 503 when fetched, so the site is treated as dead. Round date 2014-07 comes from secondary search coverage (Hypebot and Complete Music Update reporting); TechCrunch gives the $2M total and investors. Dealroom lists Andreessen Horowitz and SV Angel, which other sources do not, so they are left out. Education and individual prior employers are not sourced. Founder roles come from the YC page.
